utterances.text: Good afternoon to -- there seems to be something with the sound. Good afternoon. Good afternoon now. Everything has been fixed. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. So let's, then, find a suitable moment soon for these submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We might have in that context one question for Mr. Krajisnik as well. Yes, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just wondering, really as a practical matter, then, whether it's just going to be a matter of Mr. Harmon correcting and possibly expanding that submission or whether it might be convenient to try, according to some suitable timetable that fairly accommodated everybody, to tie that together with such submissions as the Defence would wish to make after a proper opportunity to consider the case law, Your Honour, the opportunity to consider the case law, the need for that slightly being demonstrated by exactly the sort of exchange that we've had.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then we will all come to court better equipped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, we still have the problem of the submissions of the Prosecution not yet been translated, but at least then we have a, I would say, a round -- well, at least counsel can exchange their views on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, subject, Your Honour -- I do say subject, Your Honour, to the Defence having -- of course, commitments of counsel are something to be had regard to, but also proper time for the Defence to prepare in this area is something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And I would add, Your Honour, that Mr. Krajisnik has this morning really reiterated to me that he does very much wish to have the translation of these Prosecution submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's the reason why an order was issued yesterday to have them translated as quickly as possible. One of the problems, of course, would be that the authorities are not available in B/C/S, this legal material, or would they be, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, they're available in English only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, indeed, one of the cases I tend to cite has been referenced in our submission already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: One thing I do know about English case law is it's not readily available in B/C/S, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I can tell Your Honours that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, of course, here we see one of the practical problems arising from not being assisted in legal matters. But let's not move forward; let's do it step by step. This matter having been discussed, Mr. Gaynor, it's you who's going to call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Who is a 92 bis witness without protective measures, and it is Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the witness is coming in, I'll just briefly summarise what I propose to -- the course I propose to follow. I propose to tender his two statements, tender two very brief contextual documents, read a summary of the witness's evidence, and then draw the witness's attention to a table in a third document and ask him to guide Your Honours through it briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it, Mr. Stewart, that you've received the material, also the additional material, a lot of numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think so, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Zecevic. At least, that's my assumption, Mr. Zecevic. Before giving evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. May I invite you to make that declaration of which the text will now be handed out to you by Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, you are called to testify under what we call Rule 92 bis, which means that the Chamber has read the statement you've given to the OTP and the Chamber has received some material, so, therefore, it's mainly for the public that it will be summarised. Mr. Gaynor, in view of the type of information, I take it that the summary can be really very brief, because it's not about the details, I would say, but rather about the kind of knowledge and some of the experiences of this witness. And once we've done that and once we've gone through some additional material, it's mainly the Defence who will then have an opportunity to cross-examine you. But please be aware, Mr. Zecevic, the Chamber has read your statement thoroughly. Mr. Gaynor, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll move directly to a brief summary of the witness's evidence, which I'll read for the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps establish his identity. That would be a good idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Witness, could you give us your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Berko Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I'll now proceed just to read a summary of the evidence which you gave in your statements. Dr. Zecevic is a mechanical engineer. He worked at the Pretis ammunition factory in Sarajevo from 1975 until April 1992. He specialised in the design, construction, and testing of military rockets. He was also a part-time lecturer in defence technology at the University of Sarajevo. He's a highly qualified expert in heavy weapons technology of the former Yugoslavia and has testified as an expert witness in other proceedings before this Tribunal concerning events in Sarajevo in 1994 and 1995. In his written statement, Dr. Zecevic testified about the appointment of Milorad Motika as director of Pretis in 1992. He described an incident in February or March 1992 at a JNA barracks in Sarajevo during which the commanding officer, thinking the witness was a Serb, told him that he would issue the witness a machine-gun and ammunition for free, and that the witness could come to the range in the barracks to practice using the weapon and to receive training. The witness describes a further incident in which he learned that surface-to-air missile systems, which had been withdrawn from Croatia in March 1992 and housed in the Lukavica barracks in Sarajevo, had subsequently been redeployed to an area above Sarajevo, ostensibly for protection reasons. The witness describes the imposition by the JNA of roadblocks around the Pretis factory in March 1992. The witness stopped work at the factory on the 17th April 1992. The witness had heard that there was a list of non-Serb people from the factory who were to be killed. Several days later, the JNA took over the Pretis factory. The witness learned of the existence of a list of 500 people who would be expected to continue to work at the factory; all were Serbs. The witness says that Pretis was heavily dependent on the supply of raw materials from the FRY. Without the support of the FRY, the production of ammunition at Pretis could not have continued. That ends the summary. I'd now like to tender the witness's statement of the 21st of July, 2002, and a short statement of the 18th of February, 2003, which contains corrections to the statements of July 2002, and I'd request that the registrar assign exhibit numbers to those two statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. The first statement will then get the reference P753, while the second statement will have the reference P754. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd just like to clarify very briefly for the record a couple of matters. First, we've redacted the telephone number of an individual who's named at paragraph 13 of the witness's statement. As this is a public exhibit, we want to avoid any unwanted telephone calls to that person. Secondly, I want to draw your attention to two details regarding the B/C/S version of the statement of the 21st of July, 2002. Paragraph 7, on page 3 of that statement, contains some highlighting, which I believe was inserted by a translator, which has the effect of rendering a sentence illegible. The sentence in question was clarified by the witness in his second statement of the 18th of February, 2003, and a legible version of page 3 is attached to the B/C/S statement. The second point is that paragraph 32 on page 9 of the B/C/S statement contains highlighting which obscures the date "2002," and we've provided a legible version of that page showing that the original was, in fact, 2002. Now, I want to submit two contextual documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours are now receiving copies of those two contextual documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And I'll very briefly summarise what they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: The first is a document referred to in paragraph 7 of the witness's statement and is dated the 8th of June, 1992. It refers to Milorad Motika as candidate for the directorship of Pretis, and it refers twice, in the introduction and at paragraph 2 at the foot of the page, in coordination with the SR Yugoslavia. The second document is dated the 18th of June, 1922. We'd invite Your Honours to consider that to be a typographical error; it should read "1992." Now, this records the decision of the government of the Serb Republic of BiH to appoint Milorad Motika as director of Pretis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And numbers for those exhibits, Mr. Registrar, would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. The first exhibit, reference number 3288, dated 8 of June, 1992, will get the reference P755, while the second exhibit, the decision with the ERN number 01245108 until 51 -- sorry, it's one page, will get the exhibit number P5 -- sorry, P756. I thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd now request that the witness be shown a document which is -- this has a cover fax sheet saying that this is from the director of Pretis, Milorad Motika. It's addressed to the Ministry of Defence of the RS army. It's copied to the General Staff of the VRS, and it's dated the 11th February 1993. Attached to the cover sheet -- I'll wait for Mr. Registrar to assign a number to this document. I'll request a number for that document, Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I thank you, Your Honour. This document will then be tendered and admitted into exhibit under the reference P757. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If Your Honours would turn to page 3 of that document at the top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: There's a header which says "Actual production results and manufacturing conditions in 1992." The first sentence is: "Actual output in the period from 25th April 1992 to 31st January 1993." It's shown in tabular form and expressed by a number of special purpose equipment per recipient.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Zecevic, I'd like you to turn to the table at the end of that document. It's the last two pages of that document. Do you have that table, Dr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Dr. Zecevic, were you familiar with tables of this kind from the time that you worked at Pretis?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a part of the manufacturing programme for the Pretis company, a part of the munition manufactured by this factory up until 1992 and also during the war and even now. I mean, that's what they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want you to concentrate on the header to that document and on the top two columns of the table. And you see that this is a record of items delivered during the period 25th of April, 1992, until the 31st of January, 1993. In the first header at the top, it says "JNA" on the left and then it proceeds to list what appear to be a number of brigades. Could you explain for us what that means.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This provides us with an overview for the period between the 25th of April, 1992, and the 31st of January, 1993, the names and types of ammunition supplied to the JNA and the brigades within the framework of the Republika Srpska army; for example, the Ilijas, Kosuska [phoen] Brigade, and so on. And the last column gives us the total amount of ammunition supplied over that period of time, and we've got a breakdown according to the type of ammunition involved. Do you need any further details?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I'll just draw your attention to that. The first question is: Could you give us an overall picture of the type of ammunition which is listed on the list in general terms. If you could describe what that ammunition is.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is between 76-millimetre and 152-millimetre calibre that we are talking about, and it is a highly explosive ammunition that we are talking about, fragmentation, or anti-armour bullets, depending on the type of implement used in order to launch them. We've got tank ammunition, Howitzer ammunition, and some from mortars, and guns, and rocket launchers as well. So we're talking about ammunition which has a range of a couple of kilometres -- between a couple and as many as 27 kilometres. So a wide span of ranges with regard to the effect, as well, and also the destruction between 10 and 35 metres away from the crater, in fact. And as to armour bullets, for example, some very modern ones, 125-millimetres, which were meant for certain mortars, and that was top of the range products at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I'd like to draw your attention to item number 12 as an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: And Your Honours will find item number 12 on page 6 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, you see -- would you describe for us what is -- first of all, what is the kind of ammunition described as item number 12?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Item number 12, in the usual jargon at the time, it is a 105- millimetre bullet TFG and it is a Howitzer ammunition, 105 millimetres, with fragmenting effect. And apparently 5.880 kilogrammes were supplied to the JNA, and roughly speaking 12 and a half thousand to the units of the Serbian Republic, the Srpska Republic. And the range is about 11 kilometres, and the radius is about 17 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: All right. I just want to clarify. Did you say that this records that 5.880 kilogrammes were supplied to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. No. No. It is about the quantity, the number of pieces. I'm not -- I haven't seen anything in kilogrammes. It just gives you an overview of this ammunition over this specific period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I think it might have been an interpretation error. I was just clarifying the position. Now, I want -- you said that it shows that about 12 and a half thousand of these pieces of this kind of ammunition were supplied to the VRS, and I want you just to confirm that the brigades listed at the top of this document, from number 4 until number 21, are you saying that they are all VRS brigades?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Obviously, because at that time it was only the Pretis factory from Vogosca which was under the control of the Armed Forces of the Republika Srpska. Here we've got the 27th back-up base, and it refers to the Armed Forces of the Republika Srpska and then military post offices in Koran and Romanija Corps. It is a high level, organised at the brigade level, and the Drina Corps, as well. So it was not just the brigades but the corps and individual military posts that got this ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just one more point just to clarify. Is this a record of quantities of munitions manufactured, or is this a record of quantities of munitions delivered?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. This is about the quantity of the ammunition delivered. I would like to stress this for a simple reason. According to the rules, which were applicable at the time in Yugoslavia, what was important was the fact that this ammunition was manufactured in parts, in spare parts, and there were warehouses at Pretis where all this was stored, and there were emergency plans on the basis of which they would then be dealt with and put together and completed. So the reference here is to the ammunition delivered, not ammunition manufactured. So, in other words, it is possible that more ammunition had been manufactured over the same period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Now, my final question to you. You've described in your statement the takeover of the Pretis factory, but in your statement you haven't quite given a picture of the relative importance of this factory. Could you explain to the Judges, in terms of size, what was the relative importance of Pretis as a munitions factory?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It was a key factory for the entire JNA. I'm referring to the JNA as it was up until 1992. It was one of the biggest ammunitions factories in Europe, and it had a fairly high quality rating and reliability rating. Whoever was in control of that manufacturing plant was in a position to get supplies and thus put themselves in a position of power in the course of the war. So it was not just important for the Armed Forces of the Republika Srpska or Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was quite important for the Serbian and Montenegrin Armed Forces. By way of example, even now in 2005, that is, the part of the factory that is in Sarajevo manufactures certain products for the Armed Forces of Serbia and Montenegro, quite apart from the fact that war had happened. In other words, Serbia has not been in a position so far to supplant those traditions, that technological know-how and all that. So it was an extremely important factory of primary importance in terms of the balance of power in the course of the war between 1992 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that ends this examination, and we can now proceed to cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we'll give an opportunity to the Defence to cross-examine the witness, Judge Hanoteau would like to put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I would like to refer you to your statement, the one dated the 20th and the 21st of July, 2002. On page 9 of that statement, of the English version of the statement, that is, I would like you to clarify a sentence that I don't quite understand. You said in paragraph 31, more or less in the middle of that paragraph, you say [In English] : "… of the factory was also not present and I was told that most of them were not present as they were part of Crisis Staff created within the factory. Nerkez Tanovic, who was a member of the management board and the Crisis Staff told me that his colleague ..." and so on. I should like to understand why you talk about the Crisis Staff. [Interpretation] Why do you refer to a Crisis Staff within the factory; is that really what you meant? And why would there be a Crisis Staff there? What was its role? Could you perhaps explain this a little bit, please. THE WINTESS: [Interpretation] By all means. According to the concept of the People's Defence, which was prevalent in the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, at a time when a state of emergency was declared or when political structures deemed that far-reaching changes had taken place within society, a Crisis Staff would have to be set up, and it would be made up of individuals who enjoyed the trust of political leaders, et cetera. So the usual, normal subordination system within factories would no longer apply. So these were reserve activities for exceptional circumstances. And within that framework, up until 1990, there were some special bodies or units when the Communist League was still the dominant force in the former Yugoslavia. In line with that, when it was felt that barricades were being set up, the first set in March and then in April, when it was felt that certain tensions might appear throughout the area, well, it was known who would be within that Crisis Staff, normally the director and other people from the factory. I think Nerkez Tanovic was a member of the executive committee of this factory. What I meant to say here was that after the war, when I talked to him, he gave me the following statement, and that is clearly indicated in my own statement. He said that his colleague, Branko Prodanovic, informed him that there was a list of people who were no longer appropriate, and that those people were at risk, that their lives were at risk. In line with that, he himself and a colleague, Sead Gradascevic, who was the technical manager, well, they stopped coming to work after that warning was issued. I quoted that statement to the investigator who talked to me, and I offered to introduce him to this colleague so that he could talk to him. So in other words, the Crisis Staff, institutionally speaking, was an in-built factor in all such factories, especially military factories, in case there was a crisis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the Crisis Staff would, in a way, take the place of the management, the regular management of the company.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we say that it was a kind of a purely political body then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means, because up until 1990, the entire system was under that direct control of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia. Not a single director could be appointed in the factory without the authorisation of the political or military bodies. You couldn't just compete for the post and, having met the conditions, be appointed to the post. It was essential to be the right kind of person. Certain people from the military or from political institutions had to determine that a given candidate satisfied their criteria and could pursue a certain objective that they deemed appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your statement, do you mean to say that the list of individuals who were to be eliminated was a list compiled by the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Look, in that Crisis Staff -- well, the Crisis Staff was formed long before the crisis. It was formed when a new leadership was established, and then rules were established as to how they should operate in crisis situations, and this Crisis Staff was a multinational Crisis Staff. These individuals would appear there. They worked together, they lived together, and they tried to examine the situation together. However, since the situation in April 1992 was more than just abnormal, there were certain parallel activities taking place. My colleague, Branko Prodanovic, soon left Pretis. He did not stay on in Pretis, but he was the director of Pretis at that time. He left Pretis when the crisis broke out and probably because he wanted to warn his colleagues with whom he had lived there for years. He drew their attention to the fact that there was a parallel list drafted outside the institutions, a list that said that if the crisis became worse, other people would be eliminated. This is terrible, but it's true. In the building that I live in, when in May 1992 searches were made, they found lists of individuals, not of individuals who had been eliminated but who had to be taken to the Zrak factory, which is several hundred metres from my house. They were supposed to be taken there, to be placed in a camp because they were under suspicion, and this is how certain individuals thought at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So who established these lists?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you shouldn't put that question to me. I don't know. I've been quite clear in what I have said. I have said that Nerkez Tanovic told me that Branko Prodanovic told him that there was a list of non-Serbs who had to be killed. Nerkez Tanovic or Branko Prodanovic can tell you about who compiled the list. I can't tell you about that; I just provided the source of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And one last question: This Crisis Staff in the Pretis factory, was it in touch? Did it work together with the Municipal Crisis Staff? Did their coordinate their activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It should have cooperated with the Municipal Crisis Staffs and the Crisis Staffs of other factories. It should have been under the direct control of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence because at the time special rules of conduct had been established. There was a particular chain of command, of subordination, in spite of the fact there was a multiparty system in Yugoslavia at that time. But the military structure remained the same, and the Federal Secretariat for National Defence still supervised military factories. And within the Ministry of Defence, there was a military and economic sector, which supervised or monitored military factors, and they controlled the supply and delivery of goods. And naturally, if you have a counter-intelligence officer in a factory and he has his office on the same floor where the management board of Pretis has its offices, this officer has more men of a number of men of his own in the factory, and this means that he had legal access to such premises, and these premises were under -- were fully controlled. Slobodan Barlorda was in office at the time, an educated man from Sarajevo who became engaged after he had graduated. He became a member of the military; he trained as a counter-intelligence officer. His father was a national hero from the Second World War, respected and prominent individual. But this is the role that this individual had. As far as the system of subordination is concerned, there was no particular change, in spite of the fact that a multiparty system had been established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You then may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, you say that you worked at the Pretis factory from 1975 to 1992. Did you work full time there throughout that entire period?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were a few exceptions. In 1983 and 1984, I moved over to another institute, the UNIS institute, which was a free association of military factories. They formed their institute, and then I moved to that institute and I worked in the ammunitions department. I was there for 11 months. And during that period of time, I did not work in Pretis, but the project I was involved in in Pretis was a product that I controlled from the UNIS institute from 1990 until 1992. I worked for three days in Pretis and for two days at the Faculty of Mechanical Engineering.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So was that the only break in your employment at the Pretis factory during the period 1995 to 1992 -- 1975 to 1992?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You say in paragraph 3 of your statement that -- well, what -- when you first started work in 1975, what was your position? What was the designation of your employment?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I was a project manager. I went to the research and development department and I immediately started working on a missile system, and I also assisted a colleague who was involved in Osa anti-armour missiles. I was supposed to be his assistant since he had gone away on holiday. He was an elderly man, and he soon fell ill, so I spent six months performing his duties, so to speak, and at the same time, I started working on the development of a 128-millimetre M-87 rocket. As an example, to help you understand this --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Zecevic, then. And you -- when your employment came to an end in 1992, immediately before that what was your employed position? What was the job title? A brief description.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I was the head of a department, the ballistics department, in the Pretis factory. They kept restructuring the staff. I had three engineers and two technicians who were under me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So you were still on the technical side.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I was always involved in the technical side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you say that through your work - this is paragraph 3 - you say through your work at "Pretis and my general experience in designing and manufacturing weapons, I have detailed knowledge of the whole of the Yugoslavian weapons industry until 1992." And then at the end of the same paragraph you say: "I'm therefore able to describe the entire manufacturing systems and operations of the Yugoslavian weapons industry until 1992." Now, that's what you say, but, Mr. Zecevic, can we take it that your position --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- your position, the technical or technological side meant that you were not involved in such matters as simply the buying and selling of parts, the distribution of products?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Not exactly. According to the rules adopted by the military and economic sector in 1985, in that rule book they defined the process of development and the processes involved in research. As I was involved in the development of ammunitions -- well, I have to explain this to you. Up until 1986, development was under the control of the military and technical institute in Belgrade. In 1986, the Central Committee of the League of Communists decided that the military industry had to take charge of its own development, and in accordance with that decision, I was the first person who had the opportunity to develop things on my own, in spite of the fact that I wasn't a member of the military and technical institute. What does this mean? This means that in an organised system such as the Military and Technical Institute, the development of a projectile involves the work of a number of people, and the military and technical institute had teams that worked on such things. Since later in 1986, the opportunity was offered to factories to start developing things by their own, and they wanted to become independent of the institute I have been referring to. I started work on the development of a 128-millimetre M-87 rocket, and as a result I had to do a number of jobs, more jobs than the number of jobs that people in the institute had to do. This meant that I had to spend more work -- I had to spend more time working on these things than the people in military and technical institutes. Just a minute, though --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In addition to designing and testing --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Zecevic. I certainly don't wish to stifle you from assisting the Trial Chamber in its task. It could be --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, but I have to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You do have to answer my question, Mr. Zecevic. It --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but I have to answer your question. I'll answer your question in a very simple manner. In order to take over a task, in order to become involved in a project, the military council of the General Staff has to adopt a project. You have to study the possibilities there and you have to analyse the technical aspects. You have to examine the deadlines, the prices. You have to see where you can obtain the materials, whether they have to be imported or whether you can use local materials, et cetera, et cetera. So I was involved in these matters. I was involved in developing fuel, in the production of ammunition and obtaining materials, in the course of development, and this involved the production of two to three thousand rockets. This takes two or three years, and you have to control all the stages, and you have to be familiar with all the procedures involved. You have to go to a number of factories, you have to speak to a number of people, you have to draw up contracts. In the course of development, the people involved in development would sign contracts, and I was one such person. So for 17 years I had the opportunity to become familiar with everything that was necessary in order to develop a rocket. And naturally, this doesn't mean that I know how small ammunition is produced, but as far as artillery and rocket ammunition is concerned - and that is what Pretis was involved in - as far as that is concerned, I was fully familiar with all the procedures involved. And I attended on four occasions the meetings of the General Staff, and I defended my projects at those meetings. And that is a very important role, one of the most important roles that an engineer can have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think everyone would agree that you at least answered the question, but you gave a lot of details. And whether all of these details are what Mr. Stewart is seeking is uncertain. Therefore, I can imagine that in this context you would have said something like, Since we restructured the teams that became multidisciplinary teams, including both technicians and salesmen and marketing people, and since the team being restructured worked closely together, I had knowledge of all of these aspects. That would -- at least, that's how I understand your answer to be. If you'd first give a concise answer, and if there's any further detail needed, Mr. Stewart will certainly ask for it. Mr. Stewart, you get answers to your questions though, but they were rather detailed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, to give certainty to Your Honour's comment, you said "whether all the details of what I was seeking were uncertain."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's an understatement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I wasn't. I can say I wasn't seeking all the details, to give certain certainty to that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, an understatement needs no explanation, I thought. Please proceed. Mr. Zecevic, could you please keep in mind that if you give concise answers, and if we need any further details, we'll certainly ask you for it. Yes? Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In a nutshell, Mr. Zecevic, your job was designed -- your job was to design the things, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And somebody else's job, then, was to make them?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But only after the item had been tested, and testing takes between five and seven years. And during each stage, I have to be present, during each stage of testing, those are the rules. Once the General Staff has adopted --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm sure the Trial Chamber - -without, perhaps, not being complete experts on munitions, of course, I'm sure the Trial Chamber understands that designing and testing must be part of the same exercise in relation to complex technology. We can take that, I feel confident, as a given. But subject to that, subject to your continuing input during the testing process, it's somebody else's job to actually make them once you were happy with the results of design and testing; correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, by all means. By all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's somebody else's job altogether to sell them, so far as there were markets, export markets, for example, to whom items would be sold. It's somebody else's job altogether; correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's not what it says in my statement. My statement doesn't say that that was my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Don't worry -- don't worry about your statement, Mr. Zecevic, for the moment, please. If you'd just answer my question. Is that correct? It was somebody else's job altogether to sell the things; correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And not part of your job to make decisions about where factories might be located, where production might be -- might best take place. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You were asked for advice in relation to such matters, were you?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When studying the possibilities, when analysing the possibilities - and this is what I did - we would then define or we would then establish where the ammunition would be produced, the ammunition that I had tested or the ammunition that any other expert had designed and tested. And there was a clear division. We knew which factory would be involved in the production of a given product. Pretis was involved in the production of projectiles, the calibre of which was between 76 and 150 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. You didn't participate in decisions about where factories, if that's the right word, or establishments to design and produce weapons would be located, did you?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I did, because I drafted a proposal for a decision as someone who was involved in studying the possibilities. At the end of the document, there is a suggestion made as to where certain products will be made. For example, SBS Vitez will produce rocket fuel, a detonator will be taken from Bugojno, other items by Gorazde, et cetera. This was all in the proposal forwarded to the military council.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just intervene, Mr. Stewart. Perhaps due to your first question in this respect, it seems not to be clear anymore what we are discussing. Are we discussing about where a factory would be located, that is, where a factory would be established, where a plant would be built, constructed, so that it could produce, or at what factory production would take place, that is, an existing factory? You --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're talking about both in your first question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- in your last question repeated the location of the factories.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the witness seems to answer in terms of where production would be located.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, precisely. I realise the way the witness dealt with my first question, I realise that it -- that that distinction had emerged and that therefore it was necessary to split the question or to focus on the matter of location, which is why I then asked the second question in the form that I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But it seems not to be clear to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, that's true, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Zecevic, I think Mr. Stewart asked you whether you were involved in a decision where to create a new production unit, a new factory, and he was not specifically asking you where, in what existing factory, production would be located. Were you involved in these first types of decisions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in accordance with the rules in the JNA, it was quite clear which factories should produce given types of ammunition, so that was quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll stop you. Again, the question is not in what factory to produce ammunition, but whether or not to establish new factories where one would produce ammunition.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If a feasibility study was drafted, well, the person who drafted the feasibility study would make such proposals. It's quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does that mean that you're involved or you are not involved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand what decision you are referring to, what kind of ammunition you are referring to. The Defence counsel has not been precise. There are certain rules that are in force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're not talking about rules. Let's just -- the Pretis company would need a new production facility. Would you be involved in where to locate that, to construct a new facility where they would produce ammunition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd only be involved if I was the person involved in designing the ammunition that had to be produced at this new location; only in such cases. I think I have been precise. If there was some other project, in that case someone else would make proposals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you say if you were involved in the development of the ammunition to be produced, you would be involved in the establishment of a specific production facility where that would be produced. If you would not be involved in that specific type of ammunition, you would not be consulted or be involved. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, can you just help us. What is the SSNO referred to in your -- that's the English version. I don't know whether that's the B/C/S as well, SSNO in Belgrade. It's in paragraph 6 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The Federal Secretariat for National Defence or the Ministry of Defence in accordance with the usual norms.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, you refer to an advertisement of the post of general director of Pretis in 1989 and applications by Mr. Lepirica and Mr. Bahtanovic, both of whom were apparently serving in the military at the time. The -- do you remember there was also a Lieutenant Colonel Sekularac who applied?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sekularac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I apologise for the pronunciation, but the same, Radovan Sekularac; correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sekularac didn't apply then. At the time, Sekularac was the director of the Iskra company in Serbia. He was the head of development a few years earlier, but at that time, I don't think Sekularac was in that post. Sekularac is now a director in Iskra, in Serbia, and at the time he was one of the directors in that Iskra company.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, can I try and jog your memory and see whether you can agree with this. If I put this short scenario to you, that Lieutenant Colonel Sekularac, Lieutenant Colonel Lepirica, and Captain Bahtanovic were three applicants, but then, at the recommendation of the director of production military personnel, were recommended to withdraw their candidacies because all previous directors had been civilians and it was recommended that should continue. Does that ring a bell with you?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. In what sense? Well, that's possible, but I couldn't say. I couldn't say anything about that. I couldn't say anything about Sekularac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you, therefore, have any recollection that Lepirica and Sekularac withdrew their applications, but Captain Bahtanovic, who objected to the policy, insisted that the process should go ahead with his application, remaining an alive application?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I do remember Ismet Lepirica withdrew and Bahtanovic did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And, in fact, Bahtanovic didn't get enough -- there was a voting system for this, and he didn't get enough votes to be appointed, did he?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm unable to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So you don't remember, then, that when competition for that -- open competition for that post was --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I really can't tell you how the vote proceeded.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The reason I'm putting this to you, Mr. Zecevic, is because you do give an account of this process in paragraph 6 of your statement. Do you see? You describe the post was advertised, both Lepirica and Bahtanovic applied, that they weren't appointed because they weren't supported by the SSNO in Belgrade, and then you go on to comment that for political reasons the most important departments were run by people from two particular regions. So I'm just -- if you don't remember these things, Mr. Zecevic, that's an entirely proper answer, I'm confident, in the eyes of the Trial Chamber. So do you remember or not that Mr. Prodanovic was eventually elected when the public open competition was repeated?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He was elected at the second open competition, where he was the only candidate. It was the traditional way things used to be done in the former Yugoslavia. I'd just like to tell you that if we look at the whole thing in a more general way -- well, in that case, you have to consider all the various aspects. Mr. Branko Prodanovic was a good economist, but he was a manager of a small part of the Pretis factory, which was in charge of transport vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I'm so sorry, I don't wish to be rudely interrupting, but I do wish to clear first whether what you're about to say is in any sense an answer to any question I have asked. Because if not, then we can, with respect, move on. Should we do that, then?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. In fact, Mr. Lepirica, withdrew, didn't he, just before the matter was put to a vote?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then in the next paragraph of your statement, paragraph 7, you refer to the appointment of Motika, of Milorad Motika as a general director. You say that Jovan Jovicic was in a position to propose names of general directors to be appointed at the moment important special purpose factories located within the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Then you say: "I --" well, first of all, when exactly do you say, if you remember, that Mr. Jovicic first proposed Mr. Motika?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'd have to look at these papers. There is a document, in fact, where Mr. Mocic [phoen]suggested -- it says the 8th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What says what? What document are we looking at now? Well, rather than rely on my eyesight from that distance, Mr. Zecevic, perhaps you -- and others who are further away, perhaps you could simply just --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I mean it's 01396688, the information on the possibility of renewing manufacturing in these companies. I think you might have gotten this document earlier on, at the start of this hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do I understand, Mr. Zecevic, that you've got in front of you documents that are not presented to you at that very moment to you by the party who's examining you? Because if a party examines you on certain documents, they should be presented to you and then --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I got just now. The Prosecution document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can't see what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is the first of the two contextual documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But if they are not the subject of examination, they should be returned to the registrar because it's not for the witness to make a small collection of documents he considers to be relevant. Mr. Zecevic, this is not to say that you may not refer to documents you are aware that are in existence, but you should have no documents in front of you that were not presented to you by examining counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Your Honour, that document was presented by the Prosecution a little bit earlier by Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But then they should be returned after we've dealt with them to the registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wasn't contradicting or quarrelling with what Your Honour was saying at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I was simply trying to move matters along as a matter of information. I was saying -- I've just had a look at it myself, Your Honour. It does contain different -- it's signed apparently by Mr. Jovicic and it does contain, specifically, the point about proposal of Mr. Motika to this position. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That does, in fact -- Your Honour, the document does help as an answer to the question I asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not criticising the witness for referring to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Nor I, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just trying to keep tight control over what document is in front of whom exactly at this certain moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I can only endorse that, with respect, Your Honour, because in fact the document -- in that way. So I don't -- I don't need, then, to spend time on that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But, Witness -- we get -- I'm sorry, we get so used to calling people sometimes witnesses, Mr. Zecevic, when they're to be anonymous. I will use your name. Mr. Zecevic, you say that you believe that the RS, or Republika Srpska government, complied with this proposal because the General Staff of the JNA was behind him. Now, that's just speculation, isn't it, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that, you know, because the position that Mr. Jovicic held as the president of the Association of Arms and Weaponry Manufacturers, where all such plants came together and where all directors in the last analysis, no matter who appointed them, unless there was approval from the defence ministry, well, they could not hold such a position in the first place. Mr. Jovicic was a person of some respect. He had fairly respected results to show for his work at both Pretis and UNIS, and then he was the president of an institution which exerted a considerable influence, and it was under considerable influence from the defence ministry. And it was quite normal, considering that at the time Bosnia-Herzegovina had already been recognised by the UN as an independent state. And now we have this influence being exerted by the Association of Arms Manufacturers of Yugoslavia. I mean, this is my opinion. As to whether this opinion is in line with your attitudes is quite another matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I just ask the questions, Mr. Zecevic. I have no attitude. Mr. Zecevic, when you say you believe that the Republika Srpska government complied with this proposal because the General Staff of JNA was behind him, you mean specifically behind Mr. Motika, do you? Or behind Mr. Jovicic? Who's the "him"? You're talking about Mr. Motika, are you?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In my statement, if Mr. Jovicic drafted a proposal, and the result of that proposal was that colleague Motika was elected as director, it meant that both of them were happy. I mean, Jovicic's proposal was taken into account, and the other person was appointed as director.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Zecevic, what I'm putting to you is that in stating it in terms of "I believe that the Republika Srpska government complied with this proposal because the General Staff of the JNA was behind him," you're giving some grossly exaggerated importance to this process. You don't know that the position wasn't just this, as I'm about to suggest to you: That the General Staff of the JNA didn't think very hard about Mr. Milorad Motika, and the government of Republika Srpska didn't think very hard about Milorad Motika. They trusted that when they get a piece of paper from somebody in a position of authority recommending that -- in fact, four people, four engineers should be appointed to particular posts, they let them get on with it. That's what happened, as far as you were aware, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's not correct. Because de facto, at that particular moment, Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Federative Republic of Yugoslavia were two separate states.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you know that the General Staff of JNA even gave five minutes' thought to Mr. Motika? Do you know that yourself?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think I should remind you that my statement reads: "I think that the government was in favour of this proposal." If I say "think," I don't mean I know 100 per cent. This is my opinion, and I've tried to explain the reasons behind that opinion as best I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You mention a branch office in Belgrade: "The Pretis factory opened a branch office in Belgrade." In fact, in the same paragraph, you've mentioned another company, organisation, called Unis-factories. In fact, it was Unis-factories that had a branch in Belgrade, wasn't it, and not Pretis?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. The owner of that branch office, according to the books, is the Pretis company. It was itself founded in 1948, and UNIS in 1965. That's a difference. According to the property records, et cetera, the Pretis factory is the owner of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Have you been looking at property records in relation to this matter, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. I was just on the workers' council at the Pretis company when we were looking into the matter of who was the owner of Pretis, and so I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. So the answer is you have, at some point,looked at property records in relation to this matter.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I received information about the fact that the branch office in Belgrade was indeed owned by Pretis, and Pretis was within the framework of UNIS; in other words, UNIS was the holding company. All this is, of course, arguable.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, let's stick to what might be facts that you know. It's this: UNIS had a branch. Pretis never opened a branch in Belgrade. When Pretis joined Unis-factories, it joined with an organisation that already had a branch in Belgrade; correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, it's not correct. UNIS did not exist. There were five factories which gathered together and created the UNIS company, and as soon as UNIS was set up, automatically the branch office, which was in Belgrade, came into its hands. But in terms of property relations, it was still owned by Pretis, and UNIS used the premises. I suppose that's specific enough for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: A small point actually, just on the -- the text. At the last sentence of paragraph 8 - it may be a correction needed - the English still reads: "I never detected nor heard of any discrimination against an ethnic group in a weapons or ammunitions factory, and a person's ethnic origin was never considered when he/she was employed or promoted," and I think the next word in English must be "except" rather than "exempt," so "employed or promoted except for high-ranking positions." Perhaps we can have an agreement about that, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: We certainly agree on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Grateful for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That being a minor point, I'm looking at the clock, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's perfectly suitable if that suits Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I have, however, one additional question. I would like, Mr. Zecevic, if you would agree, to ask you to do some homework during the break, although I am hesitant to ask you. In paragraph 25 of your statement, you give information about where the major weapons and munitions factories were located at the beginning of 1992. Could you please, over the break, review the list of factories in Bosnia and Herzegovina and identify for us whether they were in an area which soon after the beginning of 1992 came under Republika Srpska control or under Federation control. Would you please do that over the break, to give that some thought. But then, of course, you would need a copy of at least page 7 of your statement. I think, as a matter of fact, we'd rather keep the original in the hands of Mr. Registrar. Could any of the parties provide --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think we've got one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In B/C/S, then, preferably.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, yes, exactly that, Your Honour. And I think it's a clean copy. Your Honour, we can hand it up straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We'll hand up the whole statement, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There's no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least, I take it, Mr. Gaynor, you have no objections against that?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Certainly not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will adjourn until a quarter past 4.00. Mr. Stewart, could you give us any indication on how much time you would need?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just working it out. I thought I would need pretty much the whole of the first session, but I don't think I started until about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- quarter -- or twenty past 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Half an hour? Would that be --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's going to be a bit tight, Your Honour, half an hour. It's going to be a bit longer than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's say one hour in the next session?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It shouldn't be more than that, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krajisnik, would you have any questions, and how much time you would need for that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't really tell you at this stage whether I'll have any questions. It depends on how it goes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll, then, hear from you. We'll adjourn until quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please proceed. But perhaps not until after we have asked the witness whether he could give us some information about the location, that is, either Republika Srpska or Federation. Could we just go through it. Production of air jet engines under British licences, would that be in what territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be the territory under the control of the Armed Forces of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Production of radar and telecommunications systems would be ...?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Armed Forces of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Rockets and gun propellants?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] HVO. HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, HVO, that's Croatian. I only made a distinction between Republika Srpska and Federation, but you make a further distinction, HVO, yes. Artillery and non-guided rocket ammunition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand the Army of the Republika Srpska. Artillery fuses for ammunition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Army of the BH and HVO up until 1993 and between 1993 to 1995, the Armed Forces of the BH.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then anti-tank and anti-personal mines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same, since it's the same factory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Infantry ammunition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Armed Forces of BH and HVO up until 1993, and afterwards, the BH Armed Forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then production of combat weapons, Howitzers, and multiple rocket launchers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Army of BH and HVO until 1993, and as of then, the Armed Forces of BH.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's the same. Armoured vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Republika Srpska. The Armed Forces -- or rather, the Army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Construction of planes and helicopters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992, machines were transferred to Serbia, and the location itself was under the control of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you say under HVO control but without machinery since 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, without the machinery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Optical electronics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All three armed forces had parts of production plants under their own control, but the main part of the factory was under the control of the Armed Forces of BH. But parts of production plants were in a number of locations in Bosnia and Herzegovina, so everyone could have some of these optical instruments manufactured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then engines for military vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Armed Forces of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And finally, primers factory in Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The BH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It already mentions a location, which is Gorazde. Mr. Stewart, you may proceed. And thank you very much, Mr. Zecevic, for giving this additional information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, perhaps on that -- while we're on it, that very last point, primers factory, what's that? What does it mean, primers factory?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: These are small elements which are placed into ammunition inside bullets or inside ammunition in general, and they provide flame, and they are subsystems of systems such as ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And I hope I've got the checklist right, but then looking at the items which you said at some point were under -- or in an area of the control under the Republika Srpska, the first one was production of air jet engines under British licences. Can you just give the name of the place where it was?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Rajlovac in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the fourth one down: "Artillery and non-guided rocket ammunition."

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Vogosca, Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then I think the next one was: "Armoured vehicle plant." That's about four or five up from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Hrasnica, Famos apparently.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then the penultimate one: "Engines for military vehicles."

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Koran, Pale, and Hrasnica Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the one above that where you said that all three, by which you meant, I think, Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Republika Srpska armies, and the Croats, optical electronics. Was that in split locations, did you say, or ...?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, there was the Zrak factory, which had production plants in Kiseljak and elsewhere, Sokolac, and so on, on a number of locations. But the original production plant was in Sarajevo, and then later on they were outsourced elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the -- if all three had control of some of this, the particular location, then, that was under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska in relation to optical electronics, where was that?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, if you intended to cover all the Republika Srpska locations, did I miss the production of router and telecommunications systems?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I may have done, Your Honour. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the second.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, the second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first one, the air jet engines was in Rajlovac and then you jumped down to the fourth, which was Vagosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, that's probably right, Your Honour. Well, Your Honour is clearly looking at a list so -- JUDGE ORIE: Would you tell us where --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The same question, Witness. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The second one, production of router and telecommunications.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I'm obliged, Your Honour. Thank you. My list had slipped there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We were -- let's go back to where we were, then, please, Mr. Zecevic. I'd asked you about something which is at the end of paragraph 8 of your statement, where you say you never detected nor heard of discrimination, except for high-ranking positions. In fact, not all directors of this Pretis factory were Serbs, were they?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I ask you to give me a document with properly-numbered paragraphs? Because my document has been taken away from me, so I can't find my way around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, largely you won't actually need the document, anyway. If you do at some point, then I'm sure we can arrange for you to have one with numbered paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But actually I don't particularly wish you to have the document, or you don't need it at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Mr. Zecevic, if you first could return the B/C/S version that had been given to you by Mr. Stewart through the assistance of Madam Usher. And if Mr. Stewart wants you to read a specific part, he'll present the document to you. If not, he'll put his questions in such a way that the context should be entirely clear to you. If it's not clear, please address me or ask Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, may I -- see, the paragraph reference I'm giving is for the benefit of others who are following this from the statement in their hands. The -- well, I put it to you specifically: Mr. Abas Deronja was a director at Pretis for more than eight years, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And over a period in the -- when I say "more than eight years," a period during the 1980s and early 1990s. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But which institution are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of Pretis.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. Abas Deronja was the director of Pretis before 1965.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, all right. And Mr. Fadil Numic, was he a director for more than four years?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: During roughly the same period, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And at what point, then -- when you say that a person's ethnic origin was never considered except for high-ranking positions, at what point in the hierarchy do you say that that exception came into play?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: With reference to key positions, the company director or department managers, according to the then-system, the so-called self- management system, you had the companies, which were divided into departments. And if you talked about directors of certain departments or companies or executive committees, et cetera, a count was taken of who should be in what position. It was in line with the general policy, which was the prevalent policy in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, the so-called national key. So it wasn't an exception, if I may say so, but in the course of that process of deciding and defining who should hold what position, there was always the possibility of channeling things in a certain way and placing people in certain positions. And between 1975 and 1992, the director of Pretis has always been a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, what are you saying? Are you saying there was, in fact, a quite deliberate policy of favouring the Serb nation or Serb ethnic group during that period in relation to senior positions?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But could you please tell me which period you are referring to. I don't want to provide a lengthy answer. I wouldn't want the Presiding Judge to object to my answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Zecevic, yes. Mr. Zecevic, you had yourself referred to the period 1975 to 1992. That was the period you said: "And between 1975 and 1992, the director of Pretis has always been a Serb." And when I referred to "that period," I meant the period you just referred to. So there's no confusion after that explanation. Are you saying that during the period 1975 to 1992 there was at any time a quite deliberate policy of favouring the Serb nation or ethnic group in relation to senior positions in Pretis?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: There was such an impression, but during certain periods of time from 1975 to 1992, well, that's the period during which I was in the factory, and there were various reasons for which such things occurred. Now, whether you want me to explain this or not is up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, first of all, I put it to you that to the extent to which a person's ethnic origin was considered for high-ranking positions, it was because there was an overall policy over those years of ensuring, at least, some sort of balance in important positions among members of the different nations.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I provide you with an example? You mentioned --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, first of all, say whether that's right or not, Mr. Zecevic, and then any example which helps to support your answer.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, may I provide you with an example? That's not quite correct. You mentioned Mr. Sekularac, the third person who applied for the post of director of Pretis and then he withdrew his application. Perhaps there is something that I don't remember quite well, but as soon as he withdrew his application, Mr. Sekularac rapidly became the director of the Prva Iskra company, which is in the vicinity of Belgrade. You can check. This person who was a candidate for the post of director of Pretis was there. There were two other individuals who applied. He could -- he was able to become the director of Prva Iskra, but the other two individuals who had applied for the post of director in Pretis couldn't apply for that position. So up until 1985, 1986, 1987, there was a quite clear distinction. No one would have thought that there was a deliberate policy that was being implemented in the sense of discrimination on the basis of ethnic groups, but there was the general impression that most educated people who were employed in Pretis had been -- were people from Belgrade. They came to Sarajevo, which was a smaller town, and they had a slight advantage. But this was never an advantage on the basis of their national membership. Towards the end of the 1980s, there was a quite noticeable lack of balance. If you have a look at the leadership structure from the level of directors of sectors and upwards, you would see that in over 80 per cent of the cases, they were Serbs. In the case of Mr. Motika in the 1990s, Mr. Motika was the head engineer for explosive materials, and in two or three years he became the director of a company. This can't happen anywhere in the world. You can't have someone in an extremely important position in an ammunitions factory and you can't have a person appointed to such a position if such a person had no management experience behind him. That's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You -- and the reference is paragraph 11.
