You said that: "By the end of Tito's life, 1980, the concept of defence of the --" we're talking about former Yugoslavia –- "the Federation had started to change. The changes in the military factories also mirrored the changes in the SFRY. Although I was never involved in politics, I began to see how politicians from the various republics were using their influence to change the defence plan of the SFRY. Republic interests began to dominate over the national interests of the SFRY." You're putting it there in your statement - and is this correct - as a process of change which began right at the beginning of the 1980s? Correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. After 1980, after Tito's death. Perhaps after 1982 and 1983.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But starting, in any case, in the early 1980s. That's what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then if the politicians from the various republics were using their influence to change the defence plan, were they, broadly, all looking for the same type of change?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I -- well, what I have in mind is --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I can tell you why I made such a statement. Up until 1980, the situation was quite clear. It was clear that only a certain factory could produce a certain kind of ammunition. Pretis could produce ammunition the calibre of which was between 86 and 155 millimetres. Krusik in Valjevo, in Serbia, produced shells of various kinds and missiles. However, from 1980 onwards there was pressure that was exerted, so anti-armour rockets that were produced by Pretis were then produced by Soboda Cacak, and then anti- armour projectiles developed by Pretis were transferred to Titovo Uzice. That's where they were produced. So a factory in Macedonia was opened for launchers, and another factory was under construction for infantry weapons in Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, just one moment. At this point I wasn't seeking quite that type of detail in that sort of area. It was this: You say that "Republic interests began to dominate over the national interests." So just to be clear. The -- each -- of course, each representative of the separate republics pushed the interests of his, her, their own republic. That's what you're saying, right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it depended on the influence that a given republic had. Not all the republics had the same kind of influence. Montenegro and Macedonia and Bosnia didn't have the same kind of influence, so when compared to the influence of Serbia, Croatia, Slovenia, not in economic terms. This is a very complex issue. It's difficult for me to answer your question simply by saying yes or no or by providing you with a couple of sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me try to see whether I could understand the testimony. You say the republic interests became more important than the national interest. First question: Did you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of the state interests at the time, up until Tito's death, with regard to the locations in which factories operated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, did you say this: That the republics were seeking their own goals in economic terms or, rather, in military terms? Because you are talking about --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In economic terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you did not say that the republics were seeking independence from other republics in terms of having ammunition available to them, which would be a military matter; it was just economy. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was just a matter of economy, because a lot of goods were exported to foreign countries, to Iraq and other countries, and everyone was trying to make sure that their factory could export as much ammunition as possible in order to obtain dollars. So the interests at stake were economic interests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that at least clarifies, for me, one of the issues. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, this particular piece of your statement concerns what you have said, was politicians from the various republics using their influence to change the defence plan of Yugoslavia. And that defence plan you had yourself summarised in paragraphs 4 and 5 particularly, the first element being that, in a case of attack there would be a withdrawal of troops and vital industries into the mountainous regions of Bosnia- Herzegovina and Serbia. So that's where many of the vital weapons and ammunition factories were deliberately situated. And then another characteristic - this is exactly the way you put it - was that each of the military factories produced unique products, so they developed expertise in the designated area of production. So was it one or both of those elements, or some other element that the politicians from the various republics were seeking to change?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What I had in mind was that their primary objective was economic, and as a result, this also had certain military consequences. For example, in the case of an attack carried out by the former Soviet Union, that was what I had in mind. It's not a matter of certain republics becoming independent, develop their ammunition on an independent basis. They were primarily interested in the finances. But as a result of such an approach, the concept that was in force up until that time could be affected.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So -- well, let me put it -- for example, are you saying that whereas a key element apparently of the plan had been the deliberate situation of such factories in mountainous regions, the presumably non- mountainous republics pushed to unravel that element in their own economic interests?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you then go on to say in your statement that from 19 -- you say since, but: "From 1984/85, Serbia felt they should become economically stronger within the overall Federation, and they planned to set up some important military factories in the territory of Serbia and Montenegro to have a much larger share of weapons and ammunitions produced." You lump Serbia and Montenegro together for this purpose, do you?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were some factories in Montenegro, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Are have you done some study? Are you able to do more than approach the matter in these rather general terms?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, to tell you why I came to that conclusion, I'll tell you the following: The factory that I worked in had 5.000 staff. I was in the development and research department. There were about 30 engineers there, a total staff of 50, and we were responsible for the coordination of all the work. During that period, preparations were underway to transfer a bomb from Pretis to Belgrade. They started working on the 120-millimetre anti-armour shell. This should have been developed in Pretis, and it was transferred to Sloboda Cacak. There were some other requests, for example, for a mine to be transferred to Krusik Valjevo. There was a 120-millimetre shell developed in Pretis. They started working on it there, and then most of that project was transferred to Partizan in Titovo Uzice. And then there was the launcher for an anti-armour rocket, 190-millimetre rocket. It was supposed to be made in Pretis. It was transferred to Macedonia. And then the production programme for hand grenade was transferred from Bugojno to Montenegro, and there were many other such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Zecevic, you've given a number of examples, specific examples, that you recall of movements of facilities. In relation to -- to what you say here, that after 1984/1985 Serbia felt they should become economically stronger, that was a distinctly economic policy, wasn't it? That was what was driving it; correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. Look, 125-millimetre projectile costs 1.000 dollars. If you produce 10.000 such projectiles, well, do your multiplications and you'll see what the profit was. And this was very advanced technology at the time, and at the time I quite clearly stated that economic interests were at stake.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And so you've described, of course, that some -- all republics were equal but some were more equal than others, and Serbia was very powerful in relation to other republics, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, from the time that the SFRY came into existence, yes, it always had a lot of influence. It had a lot of educated people, many officers, officers in the JNA were from Serbia, et cetera. The capital of Yugoslavia was Belgrade. When compared to Bosnia, Serbia was at an advantage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you talk here about, in your statement, paragraph 12, Serbia starting to parallel manufacture weapons and munitions, and you say this parallel manufacture had previously not been permitted. Mr. Zecevic, every republic was in favour of abandoning strict parallel manufacture, wasn't it, if it suited that republic in its economic interests?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. At the beginning of my testimony, I said that there was a rule of the military economic sector in the Federal Secretariat for Defence, and this rule quite clearly stated how one could allow the production -- authorise the production of new ammunition. When I mentioned parallel production programmes, I said that the Pretis factory had started producing 125-millimetre shells, and all of a sudden the same sort of weapon was being produced in Serbia. They started producing the same kind of weapon in Serbia. This was not reasonable for a small country like Yugoslavia. Pretis produced 90-millimetre anti-armour shells; Sloboda Cacak at the same time started producing a projectile, the calibre of which was greater. So there was a parallel production line; that is what I'm talking about. It wasn't reasonable in economic terms to proceed in this way if you look at Yugoslavia as a whole, but if you look at Yugoslavia as a collection of republics, a sort of economic organism, then this was reasonable, from the viewpoint of a given republic. And that was what I meant to say. I always thought of Yugoslavia as a system, as my state. That was my view of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, what I'm putting to you is that it wasn't that Serbia was wanting to break this rule about not having parallel manufacturer, but the other republics were wanting to keep to the rule. It was a -- a sort of, not free-for-all, but it was each man for himself. Each republic wanted to get what it could, economically, with whatever push it could, and if that meant parallel manufacture, well, that was what they would go for. That was the position, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, that's how it should have been. But you can't provide a single example to show that a production programme in Serbia arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina, was transferred to Macedonia or to Slovenia or to Croatia. There are no such examples. That is how it should have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You say in paragraph 13 of your statement, in the middle, you say: "Before the war broke up --" it obviously means broke out. "Before the war broke up in --" I said it myself. It clearly means before the war broke out –-"in Bosnia and Herzegovina and onwards, the JNA always decided prices of single ammunitions and pieces destined to JNA and most probably to VRS, as well." Perhaps you could clarify that, because you'd agree it can't quite mean that, can it? Because before the war broke out in Bosnia and Herzegovina there wasn't a VRS, was there?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Of course it did not exist. The matter is quite simple. All military factories in the SFRY had reserve capacities for production for the JNA that had been strictly defined, and there had to be a strictly defined number of people who would be always ready in the case of war to produce for the needs of the SFRY. And in accordance with these rules and in accordance with the budget, they established what the amount of money was that could be distributed for a given factory, and this would be dealt with by correcting the prices. This was the case up until 1992. And this relates to what I said about the Republika Srpska army. Since 70 per cent of the value of all ammunition produced in, for example, Pretis had to do with imports from Serbia, then naturally those who imported the goods would dictate the final price of the product. Since the factories in Serbia were under the control of the JNA, they established the cost of production for the goods produced by those factories. And then the conclusion is that the cost of production of the factory of ammunition in Vogosca, which was controlled by the VRS army, well, this cost should have been in line with the cost established by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So, Mr. Zecevic, we're -- we're getting economic -- into economics in a way, which is straying from the question. The -- what you say in your statement is: "JNA always decided prices of single ammunitions and pieces destined to JNA." So you're talking about not the cost of --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You're talking about what was going to JNA. You then said: "And most probably to VRS as well." And we have agreed that you can't be talking generally there about before the war broke out because there wasn't a VRS. So I'm inviting you to explain what you mean, then, when you say, following on from the JNA always having decided prices of ammunition and pieces destined to JNA -- what you mean when you say "and most probably to VRS, as well." What do you say the JNA were deciding, and when, in relation to the VRS?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If my memory doesn't fail me, in June 1992 the JNA had already been transformed into the Yugoslav Army, so it was no longer the JNA. In one of my previous answers, I was quite precise. The method used when deciding on prices was identical. There were certain rules that had to be respected, and the people who produced ammunition in Pretis were the same; they were the people who were involved in production before the war, up until 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, the way your statement reads was: It was the JNA who decided the prices of ammunitions and pieces destined to the VRS. That was -- is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask you, Mr. Zecevic, did you intend to say that where prices were decided by the JNA and probably to the VRS, as well, that this happened in respect to the JNA for the period when the JNA was the important buyer of these materials, and that a similar thing happened -- at least you assume that a similar thing happened to the VRS once the VRS was established and had become a important client of these production facilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, there are many occasions on which I have acknowledged that Your Honour's question has improved and clarified mine, but I'm afraid to say, Your Honour, this isn't one of them. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please put it in such a way that we get the right answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, it certainly helps now and then to try to understand what a statement says and to try to listen to the testimony of a witness such as to elicit -- such as to better understand what a witness, sometimes not in perfect terms, intends to say. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, for five or ten minutes that's what I've been trying to do. And the question I was asking, Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I am doing. I am doing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, the question I asked you was whether you were saying that it was the JNA who decided the prices of the ammunitions and pieces destined for the VRS.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I read my statement, please? Can you read it out to me, the text of that paragraph referring to what I'm supposed to have said?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I'm reluctant to do the whole paragraph, Mr. Zecevic because --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. That part of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, you said: "Before the war broke out in Bosnia and Herzegovina," and onwards, "JNA always decided prices of single ammunitions and pieces destined to JNA and most probably to VRS, as well." That's -- perhaps, Witness, that's the sentence. Perhaps I can simply say, please clarify.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's a very simple matter. Perhaps I wasn't quite specific enough in my statement or -- but anyway, it's a simple matter. Up until 1992, they decided on prices -- the JNA, I mean, and when the Republika Srpska Armed Forces were set up, I said that it was probably the same procedure, the price-setting procedure. Because I do have the information that about 90 per cent of all elements were being imported from Serbia when it came to the manufacturing of ammunition in that period, between 1992 and 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say "the same procedure," do you intend to say that VRS, as buyer of this ammunition, similarly decided prices, or did you intend to say that JNA was deciding on prices of ammunition delivered to the VRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in order to make a bullet or any kind of ammunition at Pretis, what was needed was to import fuel, explosives, and other articles from Serbia. And they already had prices which were determined by the JNA, which meant that basically 30 per cent of the work was done by staff at Pretis and the materials were used from the storage of Pretis. But the prices of any military products manufactured by Pretis between 1992 and 1995 already included the price Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that had been set by the JNA in Serbia and Crna Gora or Montenegro or the former Yugoslavia. So that was my basic idea when interpreting all the various aspects of the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It would also determine the price to be paid by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By all means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Zecevic, is it this, in a nutshell: You're saying that because the JNA were effectively the suppliers of components, that as an economic matter their price-setting of their supplies to Pretis inevitably dictated the price at which the completed product could be sold to the VRS?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So it wasn't that the JNA was in some way taking a decision for the VRS. It was just the economic process.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If you say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, you're the witness. It's your evidence. Do you say so?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I tend to disagree for a simple reason, that there was an embargo for imports of arms and raw materials for the production of arms and ammunition for the entire Bosnia and Herzegovina. And, of course, we could discuss this matter at great length, and I don't want to waste too much of your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's no longer an economic aspect we are talking about, because importing weapons from one country to another was covered by the embargo of the UN, and any import of weapons into any country is subject to some special procedure. We're not talking about economic interests only, but about political interests, as well. So sales of arms are not only economic transactions, but they also include a political aspect, as well, and a security aspect involving the entire region in which the transfer of weapons and ammunition is carried out. It is a very complex issue indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sure in due course we can extract from those answers sufficient --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber will have to do that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You go on in your statement - this is paragraph 14, for the reference - to talk about how the contents of warehouses containing arms were gradually being transferred to Serbia from 1988 onwards. You said: "Those were the strategic stock piles of the JNA in the military factories." Do you know what the reasons were for that process?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. It is a statement of fact based on the warehouses situated at Pretis, semi-finished goods and finished products, as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you have knowledge yourself of the extent of transfer of contents of warehouses to Serbia from 1988 onwards?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I can quote one example: 800 rockets, 262 millimetres with a range of 52 kilometres, aimed -- or intended for Iraq which were stored at Pretis, that in September 1991 they were transferred to Serbia, and it should not have been done. Furthermore, ammunition which was meant for Kuwait, 125 millimetres, was also owned by Pretis; it was the property of Pretis. And there was a whole range of finished products. And from a purely objective point of view, it was all under the control of the JNA, but up until then it was customary for those products to be stockpiled and stored at Pretis. And then at that period of time, in 1988, we noticed that these stockpiles were being withdrawn. And if we add to that various implements for the production of ammunition, which was the property of the defence ministry and which was stored at Pretis as stockpiles, as reserves, that too, was withdrawn, and also documentation on microfilms about the production of ammunition, all the technological processes involved. At that time, there was copying of those microfilms, and such copies were taken away to Belgrade. That's the information that I've got.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the ammunition meant for Kuwait, when -- you say that was moved. When?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your statement in -- refers generally to movement of contents of warehouses from outside Serbia to Serbia. What degree of knowledge do you personally have of the overall extent of movement of contents of warehouses from all the other republics into Serbia in the period 1988 to 1992?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Nothing more than this, apart from rumours. But other than rumours, what I've just told you and nothing else. Because I've had the opportunity to actually witness those rockets which were brought from the port of Ploce in August 1991 and they were stock piled at Konjic, and in the course of the summer recess, that ammunition was moved. By way of example, we are talking about strategic weapons, rocket systems with sub-ammunition for anti-tank weapons and anti-armour mines with sensors, and the price of a single rocket of this kind was about 11.000 dollars. And that ammunition was not a part of the weapons of the JNA. It was meant for Iraq in 1990, because of the attack on the part of Iraq, the attack on Kuwait, there was then the embargo. And so what I've already told you about happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In paragraph 22 of your statement, you say: "I was told by Radovan Kakuca, one of my Serb colleagues, that from 1992, people of Serb origin, and organisations who were aligned to the Serb nationalistic parties, such as the SDS party, began to get weapons issued to them." You say: "To the best of my knowledge about the structure of the defence organisations in the SFRY prior to 1992, I'm aware precisely how these groups could be armed. Following the order to centralise all weapons held by the Territorial Defence forces, weapons were handed in and stored in specified warehouses. A person was appointed as the warehouse supervisor of this warehouse and had responsibility for the safekeeping of the weapons stored within it and possessed data of weapons stored." Mr. Zecevic, can we take it that all of that is information that you have got from somebody else, about which you have no firsthand knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Shall we take it step by step? Mr. Kakuca is somebody who works with me at the development institute. He was a normal person, no extremist, and everybody was worried about what was going on in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May just make a -- make a suggestion. This step by step is often a very good method, but perhaps if you could just say if there are any parts of that about which you do, in fact, have firsthand knowledge.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I was the deputy president of the rocketeers association of Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1991 and 1992, and prior to that I was the deputy of the entire organisation for the entire Yugoslavia. And prior to 1991, I got a letter in which my association was being offered several thousands of rocket engines, 70 millimetres, American production. And I went to the warehouse, and I took 500 of those rocket engines from the warehouse. It was something that,up to then, would have been inconceivable. And we went to a warehouse in Jenevica at Hadzici, and those 500 rockets were moved to Pretis, where I worked, and it was placed in a small warehouse for the needs of the rocketeer association. That's one case. And the other case, if you take the Falatici [phoen] warehouse. It is situated in Sarajevo, and arms owned by the Territorial Defence of the city of Sarajevo were sought there, as well as that belonging to all the production plants situated in that area. For your information, the arms for Territorial Defence was bought by workers from their own funds, not from the budget of the defence ministry, but the workers had to pay for it. In 1992, the JNA was in control of that warehouse, and at some point in May 1992 there was a trench -- or rather, a tunnel dug out from the other side, and all the arms were taken out of there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me one moment, Mr. Zecevic. I wonder if you would simply excuse me one moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not being wholly successful in achieving the answers being directly and proportionate to the questions. Help, Your Honour, is what I'm saying, Please. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Mr. Stewart, that depends also on the way the questions are put. And sometimes - you may have noticed this - you ask whether the witness has any personal knowledge of matter. He'll tell you about the personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's what I'm asking him for, Your Honour, about those matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has considered your cry for help. You'll get another ten minutes, Mr. Stewart, to finish your cross- examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Your Honour? I'm sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll get another ten minutes to finish your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, is that help being declined? Because, Your Honour, I've had tremendous difficulty in proceeding through my cross- examination because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you're really interested to know, for example, what -- you have spent lots of time on the final part of paragraph 11, on paragraph 12, on paragraph 13, which are dominated by statements of the witness saying -- and he answered: "The republic interests began to dominate." Yes, that was an economic matter. And then the next one was could they have profitable manufacture. In 13 we find a lot of economics. You have spent an enormous amount of time on just establishing what this already says, and what seems to satisfy you is that it's mainly about economics and not about anything else. Well, that's what the statement says. There was no need to go into that detail and to emphasise that again and again and again. So, therefore, it's also on the basis of the way you use your time in cross-examination that you'll get another ten minutes, and I'll not take this one minute off.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, do you know that on the 16th and 17th of April, 1992, Muslims broke into the Pretis factory and carried away considerable quantities of ammunition?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I know it was on a Friday evening. A Thursday or a Friday evening at some point in April.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And whatever precise date it was, then, they entered the factory grounds around 4.00 in the morning with cargo -- two cargo vehicles, two passenger cars accompanied by a police armoured car?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You never heard anything about it? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't have any information as to the armoured vehicles getting there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. Without the details, do you know that around that date Muslims broke in, they had some sort of vehicles, passenger cars, have you heard of them disarming security, carrying away seven 80 Osa rockets? Have you heard of that?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that they took anti-armoured rockets and some mines.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't catch what category of mines, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And do you know that after that attack, which was successful, they went back a short while afterwards with a larger group of about 100 Muslims and more trucks?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I know something like that appeared, but I don't know how many people or how many trucks. Why would I have to know that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you know that that second large assault was, in fact, repulsed and that they failed to carry away any of the stock?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I know that some people lost their lives entering Pretis because there is a plate in memory of those people who lost their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So you didn't consider it relevant when you gave two long paragraphs of account in your statement, paragraph 31, 32, about the events of April and lists of Crisis Staffs and the JNA taking over the factory. You didn't consider it of any relevance to mention that, that there'd been violent attack and a successful attack on this factory which had taken away some of the stock? You thought that wasn't relevant, did you?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Hang on a minute. I thought it would be important for me to say that General Divjak -- and that there was an attempt at occupation, at the occupation of Pretis on the part of the JNA, and that the general invited us as workers, engineers, technicians and so on -- he invited us to get there. I mentioned that it was a key element, and I phoned up my director, Radomir Ecimovic, at home to ask him, according to procedure, whether I should go there. I acted in line with all the relevant rules and regulations. And his wife answered the phone, Ljiljana Ecimovic, and she said that everything was under control and it was a false alarm. And it was kind of worrying to me that I, as a worker who spent 17 years working at the factory, was barred from entering the premises. That was quite frightening that I was barred from the premises up until 1996, and I entered in 1996, and all my documents, everything I had left there, had been taken away. And I have never managed to recover any of that. And all my work of 17 years had simply disappeared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I think Mr. Stewart asked you whether you thought it relevant to tell about this during your interview.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not one of the participants in all that, so I thought it wouldn't be relevant for me to mention it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just going back to -- to what you said about that account that we were exploring a few minutes ago, about how those Serb groups could be armed and weapons being handed and stored in warehouses and the person being appointed as the warehouse supervisor. And you go on to say: "I believe that invariably the person appointed was connected to the SDS party in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This person also had to obey all orders from commanders in the JNA." Mr. Zecevic, you don't know that at all, do you? That's -- that's not your own personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The question of the investigator was the following: In what way could weapons from the storehouse be taken out? That was the question. And in line with that, my answer was: "I believe that in order for that operation to be carried out, that is to say, for weapons to be taken out of the warehouse and for only a few people to know about it" -- and then the rest of my statement follows. You have to look at it within this context. Every passage of my statement is an answer to a question put to me by the investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And the answer of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, here -- and now it's my turn to ask questions. And that wasn't the bit that I was asking you about. I was asking you particularly about your expressed belief that invariably the person appointed was connected to the SDS party in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that that person also had to obey all orders from commanders in the JNA. And I was putting it to you: You just don't know that, do you?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. All I have expressed is my opinion as to how that could have happened. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart. Mr. Krajisnik, would you have any questions to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have some questions for this witness. Not many, I hope, but I would be grateful if I could have a ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, first of all, I think you've testified before in this court, in this Chamber, certainly at this moment --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my third time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The accused is allowed to put questions to the witness, as well. So just to inform you about this procedural aspect. Yes, Mr. Krajisnik, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I wanted to say is that I would be grateful if we could have a break now, a ten-minute break, so that I can try to put my papers into order so as to avoid repeating certain questions. But if that is not possible, I will proceed to put my questions to the witness now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have the second break a bit earlier than usual, Mr. Krajisnik. That means that we'll resume at five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, for allowing me to put questions to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're allowed to do so. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would first of all like to greet the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that we speak the language; although, we may call this language in a different way.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Please make a pause between question and answer for the sake of the interpreters. I have noticed -- or I noticed yesterday that when one speaks rapidly, it can be difficult. I won't put any difficult questions to you, because I'm not a lawyer. And there's another reason for which I won't put difficult questions to you: I wanted three of your colleagues to be located Branko Prodanovic, Milorad Motika, and Cekularac [phoen] Radovan.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sekularac. Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: What I have to say refers to things that they said, and these will be my questions, but let me tell you what I asked them. I asked them what kind of a man you were. This is not contained in your biography -- Just a minute, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Krajisnik. You may put questions to the witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: They spoke about you favourably, and that is why I will put questions to you in the following way. I believe that everything you will say will be the truth. UNIS was a labour organisation and Pretis was also a similar kind of organisation. We both worked in two of the best companies in Bosnia-Herzegovina; we've never seen each other before. And Mr. Deronja was the director of UNIS. Just tell me, the office in Belgrade was part of Pretis. It was Pretis's property, but it worked for all the factories -- all the departments of UNIS; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Gorazde. There were three machines for producing military equipment, capsules. They said that if you don't have such items, you can't have a bullet. And these machines remained in Gorazde throughout the war. Production was under the control of the ABiH -- or that factory was there; isn't that correct? That's where these primers were produced.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the company was under the control of the ABiH. If you don't have a primer, ammunition won't function properly, with one exception, in Vorasacuk [phoen] and Krusik Valjevo, it was possible to produce primers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I just want to repeat what your colleagues said, and this will be my only question: The only machines in the former Yugoslavia were in Gorazde. You can say that wasn't the case, but that is what they told me. Would you say that that is true or not?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Very well. Zrak Sokolac. Are you aware of the fact that part of Zrak, which was in Sarajevo, which was under the control of the ABiH, are you aware of the fact that part of this body was in Sokolac? Are you aware of the fact that this part was not in operation?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that the front line was at the very gate of Famos, and Famos had an agreement with Mercedes and didn't work?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The front line was by part of the factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know whether Mr. Alija Izetbegovic wrote his memoirs, the late Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I haven't read them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you were perfectly right when you asked the witness to make a pause and not speak too quickly, but you immediately put the next question before we have even heard the answer of the witness in translation. So would you please also make a pause, then.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you are right. Nothing is easy in Bosnia. We want to do everything very rapidly. So I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I haven't read Mr. Izetbegovic's book.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: If I told you - and you don't have to answer this - that Mr. Izetbegovic said that you produced - and I mean the Muslim side; no offence meant, but that's how we usually put it - he said that the Muslim side in Sarajevo produced shells in the wire factory. Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. In 1992 and 1993, I organised the production of ammunition for the needs of the BH army in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You have told the truth, and the truth will always prevail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you're not supposed to tell a witness that he spoke the truth or not. It's finally up for the Chamber to decide whether a witness tells the truth or not, and you may not comment on this. Of course, I'm happy that you are convinced that this witness, in your view, has told the truth, but you should refrain from saying any of these things. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I must say that the task that counsel has to perform is very difficult. I do appreciate the fact, but I will do my best to follow your advice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Could you tell me, around the 23rd of August, 1992, Pale was shelled by the Muslim side. On that day, unfortunately, my wife died. Could you explain to the Trial Chamber how it was possible for them to shell Pale. What sort of weapons did they use? As an expert, you probably know the answer.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, look, if I'm to tell you what my opinion is, I would have to know what was found at the site of detonation. That's what I did in Markale I. It wasn't possible for a projectile to be fired from Sarajevo. Such a projectile couldn't have reached Pale. In the course of 1992, a total of 110 projectiles, the calibre of which was 120 millimetres, were produced. There were bombs, rifle-launched grenades that were produced, and sometimes inflammable rifle-launched grenades. Such a shell could have been launched from Igman. That is the only possibility. I don't know how far it is, what the distance is between Igman and Pale, but if it's about 20 kilometres or more, as the crow flies, then only 130-millimetre gun shell could have been used. I don't know. I was never in Igman. I spent the entire war in Sarajevo, so I couldn't say anything about that. I'm trying to answer you as an expert on the basis of the basic information that you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Very well. So someone who had shelled that location must have had such a weapon.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Since I said that we both worked in two of the best companies - I worked in Tatar [phoen] and you worked in Pretis - and we discussed economic problems. At the time in Bosnia there were no ethnic divisions, we will try to get the best out of Bosnia. Pretis is not just the only example, but I'll provide you with another example. And I would like to ask you to tell us --

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: I just want to record an objection that the accused should ask questions and not make speeches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, sometimes it is necessary to make a short introduction to a question to put the context clearly to the witness in which context that question is put to him. But I tend to agree with Mr. Gaynor, that your introductions are too long and not limited to creating a context. Please proceed with your questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll proceed. I have an example for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: The task Pretis was assigned were the sort of tasks that companies in other republics were assigned. These tasks were distributed among factories in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in accordance with our production schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: The engineering companies distributed work between Slovenia, Croatia, Bosnia. My company was allocated 10 million dollars more than all the other factories in Yugoslavia, so could you reach the following conclusion: As a Bosnian at the time, it wouldn't have occurred to me to say that that wasn't right. Did we all strive to ensure that our republics were in the best possible position?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The production of ammunition was above all --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Could you just answer my question in economic terms.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there is no comparison. As far as the production of ammunition is concerned, there is always a political aspect. You can't divide these two issues. You can't buy ammunition on the open market. You can't buy ammunition freely. When this happens, then you'll be quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: As far as the economic interests are concerned --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: They told me that this was a self-propelled rocket, a PVO, and that you made a mistake when you said that it came from Croatia. It was in Lukavica, and it was transferred to Novi Sad. Are you aware of the fact, and are you sure of what you said in your statement?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't say it was -- it moved from Croatia. I said it was in Lukavica and that I was to take my students to Lukavica. We didn't find them there. They'd been moved at the time when I was supposed to train them in relation to the use of an anti-aircraft system.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: They didn't come from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Do you know that these systems came from Novi Sad?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of the fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd just like to remind the accused and indeed the witness to slow down between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I should have asked you -- Mr. Krajisnik, your questions always immediately follow the answer. I know it's not easy. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I warned the witness, but I'm making far more serious mistakes. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that a LAP, a light rocket regiment commanded by Mr. Dzakic, didn't come from Croatia. That's what it says here, but it's probably a mistake. Is it a mistake?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Do you know that the regiment was initiatively deployed in Trnopolje and not in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that fact. I have no such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: As far as appointments are concerned, can you confirm from the time that the communist system was in place, do you know that there was a system of appointing people on the basis of ethnic membership?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: And people who were members of the League of Communists were in a favourable position. They had an advantage; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Mr. Prodanovic said that there wasn't any kind of a list on eliminating Muslims, and this is my question for you now: Do you know where Mr. Prodanovic was in the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think he was in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes. Does this seem to be an alibi? He went to Belgrade and now he says there was no list.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. This shows that he was a good man and he warned his non-Serb friends in time. He told them to leave so that they would come to no harm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: That's your conclusion.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: If he says there was no list --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not telling you who told me about the list. Tanovic Nerkez, you can ask this man himself, that's what he told me. I didn't invent this; I relayed this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Yes, I know. But if I now said that Mr. Prodanovic now says that there was no such list, do you think that this was an alibi of sorts, the fact that he went to Belgrade? If he went to Belgrade, they wouldn't eliminate him.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you what my position would be about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Very well. As far as the Crisis Staff is concerned, could you explain something for the Trial Chamber, although Judge Hanoteau asked you about this. After Tito's death, there were a lot of demonstrations, a lot of protests, a lot of strikes, which was inconceivable. Were Crisis Staffs established at the time?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: There was a Crisis Staff that was established. There was a reserve plan for crisis situations, which quite clearly stated what had to be undertaken. It quite clearly stated what the composition of a Crisis Staff was and what sort of authority a Crisis Staff would have. You were a director in your company, so you must be aware of the fact that you had an official for National Defence and social self-protection, and you know that there were quite clear rules about how to behave in crisis situations. You must admit that in 1992, after the demonstrations, after all the tension, after the appearance of armed groups, one could no longer consider the situation to be normal. You can't compare this to the strike carried out by people who were unhappy because of the economy. So the situation was such that it was quite reasonable to expect that a Crisis Staff should operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Please forget about Pretis.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: No, but I want to ask you about something else. Bosnia and Herzegovina, when there were strikes, when there were crisis situations, were you informed of the fact that at the time various representatives of so-called Crisis Staffs appeared? At the time, are you aware of the fact?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Very well. You said - and I would agree with you - that as far as the special purposes industry in Bosnia is concerned -- Have I made a mistake again, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you're not supposed to say whether you agree with the witness or not. You can put questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: You said that in 1998 investments in companies outside of Serbia were reduced. Would it be correct to say that in Pretis, at the time, a significant investment was made? They invested into systems for producing rocket systems and other special machines, and this was the case in Brastvo and Novi Travnik, as well. They financed launchers, the Lorgan [phoen] and Orkan launcher systems, and in Sloboda and Princip Cigana Vitas [phoen] investments were made into rocket fuel, et cetera, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you like me to answer that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Are you aware of this fact?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know that such things occurred. But the situation is as follows: Lefit[phoe] is a special machine for producing chambers, and it's imported from abroad, and it was intended for the Iraq market. There was - - these projects were financed on a 50/50 basis by Iraq and by others. And the launchers in Brastvo, yes, the situation was the same. It was an enormous project financed by Yugoslavia and Iraq together. As far as rocket fuel is concerned, this is fuel -- well, a licence was bought in 1977 when President Tito was with Mr. Carter, and from 1977 to 1985 investments were made, not in 1988.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: So you agree that such investments were made?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for the record, your previous question started, at least in the transcript, you said that in 1998 investments and companies outside of Serbia were reduced. Were you referring to 1998, Mr. Krajisnik, or to 1988?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1988. That's what it says in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is that how you understood it, Witness? Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood it correctly. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is what I said, but it was probably misinterpreted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: You mentioned the Krema system.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Krema.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: I have been informed that there was no such system but that it was some sort of an improvisation, because if what you said had happened had actually happened, it would have been a catastrophe. Do you stand by your statement, or do you accept this explanation?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. SFOR units, the multinational armed units that were in Bosnia from 1996 and are still present in Bosnia have this in their brochures. I have photographs of those rockets found by SFOR units in territory under the control of the Republika Srpska army. There's Krema 1, 2, and 3. These are rocket systems with special warheads. In 1994, these items were imported from the former Soviet Union, from Russia. I have photographs here; I can show you to you if you like. And in the second part of 1994 and 1995, there was an attempt to improvise such a system, to copy such a system, but the results were not as effective. This system operated in Sarajevo. I have photocopies of orders here, orders from the Republika Srpska General Staff, in which it is stated that in 1994 in the military technical institute two such launchers were being produced. Mr. Ecimovic informed the Chief of the General Staff that General Mladic, as the commander of the army, was the only person with the authority to designate the location. I also have information on documents signed by the director of Pretis, Mr. Motika, that have to do with requests for six -- for bombs, 250 kilogrammes and 150 kilogramme bombs. I was part of the expert team that in 1995 carried out on-site investigations when the TV station in Sarajevo was attacked. I have information on various locations because the television station in Sarajevo was targeted. So there's much that I could tell you about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. It's necessary to call witnesses here who have established this so that they can explain to the Trial Chamber what is, in fact, correct.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could I just show you the photographs?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Witness, allow me to finish.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: It's not necessary for me to have this submitted into evidence, but naturally the Prosecutor and everyone else will state what their position is. Are you aware of the fact the director -- I apologise. Let me just find this part. Are you aware of the fact that Colonel Mensur Sacirovic remained behind you in Pretis?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Not Colonel but Major, Major Sacirovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Very well. Are you aware of the fact that Mr. Mensur Sacirovic was captured, maltreated, physically abused by Muslim extremists? Unfortunately, I have to say "Muslims."

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I saved him, and he was in my unit in 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: And are you aware of the fact that the director - perhaps I've accelerated again - are you aware of the fact that the previous director of Pretis, Jovan Vucic, was arrested in his flat? He was maltreated there and taken to a Muslim prison.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that fact.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I thank the witness, and I would like to thank the Trial Chamber for allowing me to put questions to the witness. I apologise for the mistakes I may have made. The work of a lawyer is very difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. Any need to re-examine the witness, Mr. Gaynor?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No need, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since the Bench has no questions to you, either, nothing could have triggered any need, but if I'm mistaking, Mr. Stewart, even if some of the questions put by Mr. Krajisnik would have raised a wish to put any further questions to the witness, I would allow you to put those questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I don't need to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then, Mr. Zecevic, this concludes your evidence in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for having come to The Hague and for your testimony given today, and I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The exhibits have been assigned numbers. Is there any objection against the admission of the exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Not from me, Your Honour. I don't know about Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My former Defence counsel is quite right. No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, it would be sufficient to just tell us the range of the exhibits. That's what we usually do. It's from P, and then you fill it in until ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. I do take that the exhibit number, and I list the exhibit. P753, P754, P75 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you'd just give us the last.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. To cut it short, from P753 to P757 are admitted into evidence. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we admit them into evidence but you number them. Yes, the decision is, as you thought it would be, that they are admitted into evidence. Then, Mr. Gaynor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, we're ready to call the next witness. I'll excuse myself, and Mr. Tieger will take over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: If that's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your next witness, let's just first check. Any protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAYNOR
utterances.text: No protective measures, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But, of course, I should ask Mr. Tieger, because you just announced that it would be Mr. Tieger. Mr. Tieger, no protective measures? Or should we -- no. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No protective measures. And your next witness to be called would be ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen. Then, Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Nielsen into the courtroom. Yes, Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, while the witness is being brought in, there's a matter I need to place on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it necessarily done before we start with the witness or ...? Because otherwise I would leave it till close to 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm happy to do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because for the witness it's not ... I wanted to say good afternoon, Mr. Nielsen, but I should say good evening, Mr. Nielsen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good evening, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration, and may I also invite you to put your earphones on because sometimes you get instructions to speak more slowly, and that's usually done through the earphones.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Nielsen.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The Court has received your CV, so I will not go into that, unless the Court is for some reason interested in further detail. I note that it reflects your doctorate -- Doctor of Philosophy degree with distinction, but as has been the custom here, I will refer to you by the simple title mister during the course of your testimony. The Court has also heard from other witnesses who were members of the LRT or leadership research team, and so I will try to be brief with the background that led to the submission of your report in this case and your upcoming testimony. First of all, is it correct that you were a member of the leadership research team for the OTP of the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you began your work when?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN
utterances.text: I began my work here in mid-June 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And is it correct that you are no longer employed by the OTP but are employed by the International Criminal Court?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that has been since when?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN
utterances.text: I've been employed by the International Criminal Court since August of 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, your work with the LRT involved conducting your own research and assisting the research of others for the LRT?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And is it correct that that work involved the collection and analysis of documents related to the conflict in Bosnia, and more specifically in your case, to the Bosnian Serb Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did that -- did you produce a report that focused on the structure and activities of the Bosnian Serb MUP or Ministry of the Interior during the year -- years -- well, the year 1992, but with the background of the steps leading up to the establishment of the Bosnian Serb MUP?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And is it also correct that that report was based on, in large measure, on the extensive collection of original documents in the possession of the OTP, many of which originated from the Bosnian Serb MUP as well as other source materials which are identified in your report?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if the Court would wish to mark the report with an identification number at this point, or the relevant documents with an identification number, or would wish me to proceed otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's no need to -- the report has been presented to the Chamber, this expert report, so therefore it's part of the submissions. If later we would want to assign a number to it, we may do that, but at this moment there's no need to proceed to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, in part, your report addresses some of the steps leading up to the division of what was the joint MUP and establishment of the Bosnian Serb MUP, from approximately the paragraphs 7 through 90 in the report. I'd like to simply focus on a few of those steps that you identify along the way, and I'd like to begin by drawing your attention to an item found behind tab number 1 of the presentation binders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are the presentation binders already provided to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't believe they have been, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And while they're being distributed, I can indicate to the Court that there are three binders containing 78 tabs. A further note, that approximately a dozen of those tabs have been withdrawn; although, for purposes of continuity, the numbering remains. And, in addition, another approximately dozen of those tabs contain items already in evidence. And as we go through, I'll attempt to identify those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would have to go back exactly to the guidance we Gave, but it was a substantial reduction of the numbers of exhibits to be shown and also some guidance for the Defence, how to deal with footnote material, et cetera. But let's first continue and see where we go. The most important is that first of all the witness receives the binder we'll talk about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, I had just focussed your attention on the intercepted telephone conversation contained at tab 1, which is a conversation between Dr. Karadzic and Vitomir Zepinic on 24 July 1991. Before we play a portion of that intercepted telephone conversation, perhaps you can tell the Court who Mr. Zepinic was.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN
utterances.text: Yes, in this case, Vitomir Zepinic was, at the time of this telephone call, the deputy Minister of Internal Affairs in the SR BiH MUP; that is to say, the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And was he the highest-ranking Bosnian Serb official within the joint MUP?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the transition from witness to witness was a little more abrupt than is often the case with a witness with this many documents, so we're now attempting to find the Sanction -- the intercept in Sanction, and if we can't, then we'll move on and address it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If it cannot be found quickly, I'd rather you to move on, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. And we'll return -- It's been found.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters can't find this text anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, let's restart it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: My apologies, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you would tell us where you'd start --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- then the interpreters, who have been provided with the transcript, I take it, could find the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I didn't realise that the clip portion had not been made known to them before. That's found at page 8 of the English translation, toward -- it's the fifth speaker's box --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- down from the top. And it begins with the line: "Please be sure no one is appointed without all the Serbs giving their opinion on that."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we restart, then, there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: THE INTERPRETTER: [voiceover] "K: Please be sure no one is appointed without all the Serbs giving their opinion on that. Z: All right. K: Nonsense, that man intercepted the premises here, without authorisation he inter ... intercepted the premises and he intercepted-- I mean, ran ... ransacked the food there, thinking that we were piling up weapons in Sokolac, mother-fuckers. Z: What did they give them -- K: Yes, I beg you, I'll call Devedlaka now to -- to see what he thought there, when he suggested him. Z: -- I -- in ... to see what it is. K: I'll call Devedlaka to -- to ask him what kind of ... and if Devedlaka's doing that without consulting with us ... well, he cannot suggest that without consulting with us. Z: Well, the people from Romanija suggested it to him. K: They are not allowed to, this is the personnel of the Serbian Democratic Party. I'll find him now and I'll tell him not to do these things on a provate basis ever again. Z: I'll find him. You don't have to ... K: No, it's fine. They'll find him easily. Z: Yes. K: All right. Please, let the collegium meet every morning and clear all that out. I was with Izetbegovic last night and with Zulfikarpasic. And I told him, right into his face, we'll establish a parallel government, parallel police. We'll withdraw our people and they'd have to be paid by the governemnt. We'll withdraw all our people under arms. We'll establish an entire parallel state wif you keep on screwing us. And he just looked and blinked, because we'll do that. Not even God could stop us in that, because they started to fuck with us and to fuck us up. And there's no doubt, we'll do all of that in a week. So let there be war. Let there be war. But we'll finish the job for once."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, were you able to find the B/C/S part of the ...?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was quite unable to find it. But you don't need to play it again. I've heard it. But perhaps in the future if Mr. Tieger could tell me exactly where it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, focussing in particular on the latter part of the conversation -- the latter clip of that part of the conversation, can you tell us what the discussion between Mr. Zepinic and Dr. Karadzic was about.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN
utterances.text: Well, the first thing to note about this conversation from the point of analysis is that there are two versions of this conversation that we have in evidence, both of which stem from July. However, I do footnote that in my report in footnote 24. What they're discussing here is consistent with the general expressions made by Radovan Karadzic during this time period with respect to the Serbs who worked in the SR BiH MUP. Karadzic had formed an opinion that the SDS was the legitimate and sole representative of the interests of the Serbs who were employed in the ministry. As such, the SDS party was supposed to engage in scrutiny of any appointments involving Serbs. This is the gist of what he is expressing in this conversation when he refers to his conversations with Devedlaka. Karadzic was in particular concerned about the appointment of Serbs who did not enjoy the full support of the SDS or did not agree fully with the SDS's party programme. In -- further in this conversation, we see one of the earliest expressions by Karadzic himself about a possible alternative, parallel police, as he calls it in this conversation, indeed a parallel state, if the demands of the Serbs as expressed by the SDS, again, with -- specifically here with respect to the police, were not taken seriously and were not agreed to by the other two sides. Those two sides, of course, being the SDA, the Muslim Democratic Party of Action, and the Croat Democratic Union; although, in this conversation he does only mention the SDA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. Could we be told who Devedlaka is. Could the witness please specify who this person is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point I cannot specifically say who Dragan Devedlaka was. I do know that he was a Serb who was employed in SR BiH MUP at the time. I believe in State Security Service, but I would have to check on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, you spoke about the assertion that a parallel police and a parallel government would be established. Did you report -- did your report look at documents that also considered that possibility during 1991?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Just in relation to that, to quote the evidence properly, the evidence of the witness was a possible alternative parallel police, as opposed to the way Mr. Tieger has expressed it. The assertion that a parallel police --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
