utterances.text: Ms. Loukas, is your microphone on?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. It's perhaps a little --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it's one far away from you. Could you please repeat what you said because I'm not quite sure that everyone could understand it.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's just in relation to Mr. Tieger quoting back the evidence of the witness. Mr. Tieger's question was: "You spoke about the assertion that a parallel police and a parallel government would be established," but, of course, the answer that the witness gave was "possible."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I think the witness said "a possible parallel."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I was actually referring to Dr. Karadzic's statement: "And I told him right to his face we'll establish a parallel government, parallel police. We'll establish an entire parallel state if you keep on screwing us." I consider that an assertion, and that's what I was referring to as a general matter, and clearly my question could not be taken as evidence, and that really is an unnecessary objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: With the greatest of respect, even when one does quote from the telephone conversation, it's quite clear that it is conditional. There's an "if" there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me -- but apart from that, Mr. Tieger, you said: "Mr. Nielsen, you spoke about the assertion that a parallel police in --" I have to check that first.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll withdraw the question. I'd really like to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, did your report examine documents from 1991 which considered the prospect of a -- dividing the joint MUP into separate ethnic Ministries of Interior?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN
utterances.text: Yes, the report did focus on several such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I could direct your attention, then, to one such document, located at paragraphs -- or which is discussed at paragraphs 33 through 39 of your report. And if I could ask you to turn your attention to tab 2 of the presentation binder, number 1. It's binder number 1, tab 2. That contains a document entitled "Possible ways of decentralising Internal Affairs in Bosnia-Herzegovina." Can you tell us briefly, Mr. Nielsen, what subject this paper addresses and its significance.

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN
utterances.text: Briefly speaking, this report is a report written anonymously; it is also undated. But it is written by a person or persons with a very detailed knowledge of the operation of SR BiH MUP. The person or persons who authored the report are writing from a Serbian perspective, and they're considering the possible consequences of the decentralisation of Internal Affairs organs in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It bears mentioning here that those organs were at that time quite centralised according to the laws that were in force at the time, and the document assumes that the current security situation and therefore the state of internal affairs in Bosnia and Herzegovina is in a state of flux and attempts to propose possibilities of restructuring Internal Affairs to deal with that deteriorating security situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And what conclusions does the document reach or propose?

utterances.speaker: CHRISTIAN NIELSEN
utterances.text: The authors reach a kind of two-tiered conclusion that is in is of itself somewhat contradictory. Let me explain. At the outset, they take as an assumption, as I said, that there is a deteriorating security situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that all of the three main ethnic groups in Bosnia and Herzegovina are, in fact, facing danger as a result of that situation. What is considered here is -- in particular, at the outset, is that decentralisation per se, that is to say, an environment in which each of these three communities would go about forming their own Internal Affairs organs, would actually lead to an additional, an accelerated deterioration of that security situation. The authors, therefore, retreat and ask whether there is any other ways in which the security situation can be improved, and they look at it again, as I stated, particularly from the Serbian perspective. In paragraph 36, I refer to the first tier of conclusions, which are four steps that assume the continued existence of a socialist republic MUP in Bosnia and Herzegovina; however, again, with the context of certain steps that would be taken by Serbian deputies in the SR BiH Assembly, certain steps that would be taken with respect to a cooperation with the Serbian autonomous areas, the SAOs that have been formed. That is the first -- those are the first tier of steps, as well as the cooperation with the Federal institutions in Belgrade. However, the authors go ahead and consider that it might be impossible to implement any of the -- or at least very difficult to implement any of these four steps that I mention in paragraph 36, and therefore, just to finish, in paragraph 37 they refer to four other steps which -- or, excuse me, three more steps, which are more drastic. These steps culminate, as you can see in point 3, with the establishment of a Serbian Ministry of Internal Affairs at the republican level.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I'm looking at the clock, and I remind myself that Ms. Loukas would like to address us briefly as well. Would this be a suitable moment to stop?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If the time is needed, Your Honour, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's three minutes to 7.00. Mr. Nielsen, we have to hear -- I take it not in the presence of the witness, necessarily, Ms. Loukas?

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Nielsen, you're excused. You are instructed not to speak with anyone about the testimony you've given until now and which you're still about to give. We'd like to see you back tomorrow in the afternoon, a quarter past 2.00, same courtroom. Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Nielsen out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Loukas.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Just in relation to the situation that the Defence team finds itself in. As Your Honours are well aware, we've made two adjournment applications, and of course the second was subject to an appeal, and I can't quarrel with that. Nevertheless, Your Honours have indicated that you would wish to monitor the situation, and Your Honours are well aware that our contention is that we are an underresourced, understaffed, and time-poor Defence team. And, Your Honours, I do wish to give you a practical example of the way in which Mr. Krajisnik's right to an effective defence and a fair trial is, in effect, being undermined. And that is that in our attempts between lead counsel and myself to ensure that we cover every possible base, Your Honours will have noted that of necessity it's very rare for both of us to be in court. So I will be in court for stretches of times with witnesses whilst Mr. Stewart is attending to out-of-court work, and Mr. Stewart has been doing the same, for example, in recent weeks, while I am attending to other matters that are necessary for Defence preparation. Now, of course, in those situations Mr. Stewart was not in a position to inform me, because of the strictures that we operate under, that I would be dealing with this witness until late on Thursday evening. That means that I have had Friday, the weekend, and up until today to prepare for a witness of this significance. Now, Your Honours, it could not be said, and I could not say as a responsible and conscientious professional, that I am properly prepared to deal with this witness. And that is a matter that the Trial Chamber should be made abundantly aware of. The nature of the report, the extent of the documents, there's over 500 footnotes with associated documents to be examined and what have you. Your Honour, I don't want to put myself Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. forward as some sort of unrealistic perfectionist, but at the same time, Your Honour, it's important that we do not fall below what we consider to be, as a Defence team, minimum standards in relation to preparation for the defence of our, it seems, "former client." In those circumstances, when one considers the time that the Office of the Prosecutor have spent preparing this report and the time that we have available to analyse the report and prepare for the cross- examination of the witness, again, Your Honour, we are placed in the David and Goliath situation which we are constantly placed. And in those circumstances, Your Honour, I think it's crystal clear as an example what the implications for a fair trial are for Mr. Krajisnik, and also to place it on the record as part of the background to why Mr. Krajisnik has made the application that he has made to represent himself. And it is my duty as a responsible and conscientious professional to place that on the record, Your Honours, and I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for doing so, Ms. Loukas. You're right. The Chamber has expressed that it will continue to monitor the situation. Therefore, I thank you for drawing our attention to this, what you call an example of what you consider to be a more permanent situation. Is there anything else to be raised at this very moment? Yes, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. LOUKAS
utterances.text: Not on my part, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, we are already past 7.00, so if you could please keep it as brief as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, I did want to raise one matter, something that I mentioned to Mr. Tieger the other day, Your Honour. Since he's here and I'm here. It will just take 30 seconds. It's that this was on the 26th of May, and this at page 13444 of the transcript in relation to the Trial Chamber's decision on Witnesses 681 and 682. The Trial Chamber said it would be fair to allocate to the Defence a total of four extraordinary non-sitting days for the preparation of the cross-examination of those witnesses and said, and I quote: "It's for the Defence to decide how to split this time and to inform the Prosecution as soon as possible." That was last Thursday. Now, Your Honour, we were waiting, among other things, for information in accordance with the Trial Chamber's direction which, in fact, reflected a long-standing request from the Defence for information from the Prosecution as to the timetable and schedule and hours left for its witnesses. And then on Monday the Prosecution gave me a projected schedule in which they had selected four days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Without any consultation whatever with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that this is subject to further negotiations in view of the ruling of the Chamber, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we understood, I think quite reasonably, that the Court's reference to the Defence's discretion about how to split that time meant they could use four days for one witness, two days for each witness, three days for one, one day for another. We did not understand it to give them authority over what is, in any event, a very difficult schedule to arrange.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I haven't got your schedule in my mind at this moment, but are all four days off prior to the first witness to appear?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Tieger's comment makes no sense whatever of the Trial Chamber's request that we should inform the Prosecution as soon as possible. They couldn't have sensibly read it that way, because if it was a decision for us internally to decide how to use those four days, we would have no business informing them of it. Your Honour, it was quite clear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you could have --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- that the Defence -- the Defence simply assumed that we would have exactly the opportunity indicated that we, who have very little control over this schedule, but in this particular area, we were expressly given this and the Prosecution without -- no consultation whatever with us simply presented us with this schedule and has chosen the days for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll check it in the transcript, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I've read it, Your Honour. It's there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, of course, the Chamber certainly had in mind whether you would need four days for one witness, then of course that would -- if you would have split it up in three days and one day, or in two days and two days, this would have consequences for the scheduling. But if all four days would be prior to any of these witnesses to be called -- but then even it might have been a better way to do it, Mr. Tieger, to seek the advice of the Defence and say, "Would you rather have them early or late?" I mean -- well, 24 hours is 24 hours, but nevertheless it sometimes is easy to fit in or it's not good to have four consecutive days where you'd prefer to have two days. For example, because you could continue to work on the weekend and work on the same issue. So, therefore, is there any way of further considering -- because -- consider to listen to the Defence and see what wishes there are to see whether they can be met? I'm not asking for days of negotiations. I'm just trying to see whether this matter can be resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course I wouldn't rule it out without making every effort to accommodate everyone, and I'm prepared to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I will -- to the best of my recollection, those days do, but weekends, by the way. Nevertheless, we'll take a further look. We'll do whatever is possible. But I reiterate that it's a very tight schedule dealing with witnesses who have been consulted over time, and there are strictures that are outside the Prosecution's control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: However, we'll certainly do our best, and I'm happy to look at it again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Looking at it, the first two compulsory recess days would be the 6th and the 7th of June; the next ones, the 14th and the 15th, as you scheduled them. Could you please speak with Mr. Stewart, see whether you could resolve the matter. If not, of course, then -- and in the meantime I'll go through the exact wordings I used. But certainly one of the most important things for the Chamber that we had in mind is that it was not for the Prosecution to say, Here, you've got two days. Now we go with the first witness; whereas, the Defence might have preferred to spend four additional days on that witness, and not having them all available. That was certainly on our mind. But I'll have a close look to the language we used, and in the meantime, I take it that some conversation between you might also assist in reaching a solution. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I say that -- I've said this before. Of course the -- the Trial Chamber must look at the transcript. But when counsel has read from the transcript, the implication that it needs checking to see the wording is -- verges on the offensive, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I read from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, of course I did not want to say anything like that. I just want to have time, if possible one minute, to just check in the transcript exactly what we said, and that's something we'd like to do. And in the meantime you see whether you can resolve the matter together with Mr. Tieger, and then we'll try to make the best out of it. That's the situation what we are in, and there's no need even to think about -- that I would not trust you if you quoted the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I accept that, then, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then is there -- I -- Mr. Krajisnik, I now have even to stress more that you should be brief. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to act in line with your instructions. My suggestion, Your Honours, is as follows: I agree with my former Defence team. One day should be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you can trust the Defence team. The ruling of the Chamber might be perfectly clear to you. Yes, please -- or is it -- I take it at least that when you're talking about your former Defence team that you're not referring to Mr. Brashich and Mr. Kostich, or are you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have full respect for the Trial Chamber. I was just trying to make a joke, and, of course, I do realise that they are my Defence team, even now. I hope I haven't been misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... or a joke. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've almost forgotten what I was going to say, Your Honour, but let me suggest the following: Perhaps one day could be used by the Defence team, together with the Registry, and one of your people. I know that a very wise and intelligent man used to sit somewhere there, as well. So they could perhaps look for a way of solving this problem. I mean, we don't need to talk at cross-purposes, and I think the person I was referring to is Hartforth or something like that. So together with the Registry representative, they could sit down together and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. come up with a proposal -- is that correct? That this is the person's name? So, that would be my proposal: for them to sit down together and sort things out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but the name is not exactly right, but I do understand to whom you refer. And sitting together with the Registry to resolve what problem exactly? The funds you wanted to be informed about or ...?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this Defence team could just sit down with them, and they will find a solution. I don't know how. If I did know, I would suggest it myself. There are loads of problems; they will sort something out, and then the Trial Chamber will find it easier to reach a decision. But things must work properly. So that's my proposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your suggestion is understood that you're inviting the Chamber to see whether Mr. Harhoff, as he's called, our senior legal officer, could play any active role in resolving at least some of the problems we are faced with at this moment. The Chamber thanks you for this suggestion, and we'll see whether we can give it a follow-up. If there's nothing else, I regret that I have to apologise again to the interpreters and the technicians. We'll adjourn until tomorrow, quarter past 2.00, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 2nd day of June, 2005, at 2.15 p.m.
